analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run universal health service providing free comprehensive care to everyone in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and no committee vote; it was referred to four House committees in April 1997 and died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the existing health care system with a government-run United States Health Service. Every person in the country would be eligible for free care — doctor visits, hospitals, dental, mental health, drugs, eyeglasses — delivered by salaried government health workers. It would be funded by new income taxes on individuals and corporations, and it would repeal Medicare, Medicaid, private employer health plans, and most other existing health programs. Governing boards, elected partly by patients, would run it from the community level up.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone in the United States, including the roughly tens of millions then uninsured or underinsured, would get comprehensive care with no charge at the point of service, no premiums, and no denial for pre-existing conditions. Workers would earn one hour of paid health leave for every 35 hours worked. Low-income communities and rural areas, named in the bill's findings as underserved, would get new facilities and staff through national planning.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Declares all individuals in the United States eligible for health care and supplemental services, provided without charge and without discrimination, including hospital care, dental, mental health, long-term care, prescription drugs, and even eyeglasses and hearing aids [S2][S3].

Requires each community board to provide comprehensive primary care including pregnancy and abortion services, 24-hour emergency care, and preventive services, with a general hospital in every district and a highly specialized facility in every region [S2].
Amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so workers earn one hour of paid health leave for every 35 hours worked, usable when they or a dependent need care [S3].

States in its findings that the existing system's 'unnecessary and excessive profits and administrative expenses have inflated the cost of health care,' and would replace private billing with salaried health workers funded by progressive taxes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals and corporations would pay new income taxes on top of existing rates, and the tax break for employer-provided health coverage would end. Private health insurers would lose their core market, employers would lose the ability to offer competing coverage, and doctors, nurses, and other providers would become salaried employees of the Service, barred from private practice in its facilities. Medicare, Medicaid, VA, CHAMPUS, and federal employee health insurance would all be repealed in favor of the single new system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, insurers, employers, and private providers

drawbacks.text: The bill would repeal Medicare, Medicaid, veterans' health care, CHAMPUS, and federal employee health coverage and fold everyone into a single new, untested system, so a design failure would leave no fallback for seniors and veterans now covered [S2].

It would prohibit health board facilities from being used for private service delivery and bar board employees from outside private practice, eliminating the choice to see a non-government provider for covered care [S2].
It imposes additional income taxes on individuals and corporations and repeals the exclusion for employer-provided health benefits, a large new tax burden even as premiums disappear [S2].

The plan requires building a general hospital in every district of roughly 100,000-500,000 people and a health school in every region, an enormous construction and staffing undertaking whose cost and feasibility were not detailed in the bill's $4 billion startup authorization [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Free, universal, comprehensive care with no insurers or billing would be a bigger guarantee than any health system in the U.S. today, and the bill's elected community boards and patients' bill of rights gave users real voice. The cost side was genuinely heavy: a new national tax, the elimination of every existing public and private health program at once, and a government monopoly on delivery that left no private option for covered care. Whether the disruption would be worth it was a fair question the bill never got to answer, because no committee or floor vote ever considered it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees when introduced, then to subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ron Dellums introduced the bill on April 17, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the Committees on Commerce, Ways and Means, the Judiciary, and the Budget [S5][S1].

On April 29 it was referred to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Health and Environment; on April 23 a portion had also been sent to the Subcommittee on Trade, likely because the bill repealed the Tea Importation Act [S5][S2].
No hearings, markups, or votes were ever recorded on the bill in any committee, and it received zero cosponsors [S5][S4].
The bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, never reaching a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health system was preserved: private insurers kept their market, employers kept their current benefit arrangements, and providers kept private practice. Ordinary people, including the uninsured, gained nothing concrete.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing health industry and status quo

for.name: Rep. Ronald V. Dellums
for.role: Sponsor, U.S. Representative for California's 9th District
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; a long-time advocate of a government-run universal health system.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Subcommittee on Health and Environment)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Budget Committees
against.what_they_did: Received portions of the bill with jurisdiction over its financing and legal provisions and never acted on them.

against.name: Members of the House (both parties)
against.what_they_did: None of the 435 House members signed on as a cosponsor, leaving the bill without any stated support beyond its author.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or cosponsorships, so no partisan lineup exists in the record; the sole sponsor was a Democrat and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have voided employer health plan obligations and replaced private coverage with free public care, eliminating the core private insurance market. Because nothing passed, insurers kept the status quo they profit from.

Health boards could not let their facilities be used for private care, and Service employees were barred from private practice; the bill also guaranteed employment for existing health workers within the Service. The industry would have been absorbed or displaced.

A National Pharmacy and Medical Supply Formulary would set which drugs are covered, and the National Board was authorized to operate its own drug manufacturing facilities — a government competitor — while guaranteeing free drug coverage that creates enormous public demand. Nothing passed, so current pricing arrangements continue.

Employers would owe new health service taxes but would be freed of any contractual or legal obligation to provide health coverage to employees, since the Service covers everyone. Workers' compensation programs would also stop paying for health care the Service provides.
